lines.text: People whose inner life is empty may of course very easily
fit into an organization, but they are incapable of genuine
love and fellowship. The sign of our being something of
value within is our capacity for receiving and giving love.
A poet, Wilhelm Busch, with his vein of playful fantasy,
describes with somewhat grim humour a dream which trans-
ported him into mathematical worlds. There he meets,
instead of human beings, mathematical figures who,
inwardly hollow, yet live a ghostly life like that of men. Thus
with mocking irony he holds up a mirror to our human
world, challenging men to reflect and reconsider. Is not our
life as a whole threatened by the danger of being more and
more absorbed in the organization, instead of being part of
a genuine community of true persons who mean something
intrinsically and so also can signify something for other
people? Modern life increasingly crowds out times of pause
for self-communion, for silent meditative heart-searching in
face of eternity. Many people are overcome by boredom
when the rush of activity ceases, whether it be that of work
or that of pleasure; and few men can any longer bear to be
alone. Solitude seems to them tedious. And is it worse in the
eyes of God to steal or to transgress a moral commandment,
than to grow bored? Yes, there are people who dread being
alone and take refuge in a round of activities which give them
no time for thought. They escape from themselves in sheer
noise which stupefies their ability to think.
II
But how do we come to ourselves? How do we become our
true selves? When we listen to the voice of eternity: "Behold,
I stand at the door and knock." Eternity stands at the door
of our souls with its summons. It asks us whether we are a
true person or whether we have lost our souls in our pre-
occupation with the things of time. Is this a fantasy which
we should reject as making us weakly incapable of attending
to the demands of the moment, of getting on with the task in
